title: Conferences, Catch-ups, and Clio’s Big Swing at Big Law
author: Greg Lambert · Marlene Gebauer

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Lambert identifies prospective AI-driven matter workflows and treats them as realistic but not demonstrated. He does not address whether automation weakens apprenticeship, associate leverage, partner succession, or whether firms should explicitly fund training and broaden career paths, so his position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source excerpts address conference impressions, travel anecdotes and listener outreach, but provide no substantive claims about organisational adaptation, human control, legal AI’s effects, employment, pricing or implementation. There is therefore insufficient evidence to determine a position relative to the cluster proposition.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s case for disciplined implementation by identifying a concrete confidentiality and data-exposure risk from ChatGPT settings. It reinforces the need to scrutinize privacy controls and user practices, although it does not assess vendor-market expansion, product selection, adoption or commercial outcomes.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s assistance-oriented, human-governed model and materially extends it by identifying retrieval infrastructure, data hygiene and frequently revised governance as operational prerequisites. Its proposed intake-to-workflow uses also exemplify selective deployment in bounded processes, while confidentiality risks reinforce the need for controls rather than autonomous reliance.
qs: Like you have to have, you know, data hygiene and data cleanup in order to make  you know, your AI work well.
You’re gonna rely on it for maybe six months, and then you’re gonna have to change it again.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between expanding AI offerings and realized value: Lambert presents AI-initiated matter workflows as prospective rather than demonstrated, while Wilson-Griffin’s disclosure example reinforces the need for governance and control over lawyers’ use of public AI tools. It does not substantively address workflow performance, renewal economics or consumption costs.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source supports selective, context-aware adaptation rather than indiscriminate release chasing. Lambert cautions that vendor activity often reflects competitive imitation, while Gebauer presents governance as continuously evolving and recommends organisational support to reduce shadow AI. Its workflow examples are prospective conference observations, not measured validation.

kp.k: Public ChatGPT sharing creates confidentiality and reputational exposure
kp.d: Cheryl Wilson Griffin reports that, last month, at least 110,000 full ChatGPT conversations became public, Google-indexed and permanently archived because of a checkbox. She describes an allegedly identifiable lawyer and multinational energy client whose conversation sought to exploit indigenous landowners’ lack of valuation knowledge. She frames this as professional and reputational exposure, calling it searchable malpractice; the transcript does not independently establish the incident or a malpractice finding.
qs: Last month, the world was made aware that at least 110,000 full ChatGPT conversations were made public on the web, crawled by Google, and permanently recorded into the internet archive due to a simple checkbox and ChatGPT
we have entered the era of searchable malpractice.

kp.k: Clio targets Big Law beyond its traditional customer base
kp.d: Lambert reports that Clio is pursuing larger firms following its vLex acquisition plans, with $900 million in funding. At the time of the discussion, he believes a European approval, possibly Spain’s, remains outstanding and could clear imminently. This is a report of vendor strategy and anticipated transaction progress, not evidence of successful large-firm adoption.
qs: they wanted to share those, not just with their typical customers, which typically are small, solo firms, they’ve got $900 million to play with now with funding and they’re really taking a big swing at Big Law.
I think they’ve cleared all the hurdles except for that. That’s supposed to be clearing any day now.

kp.k: Matter management could provide Clio’s large-firm entry point
kp.d: Lambert argues that large firms lack adequate matter management software and predicts Clio Operate could enter through this gap rather than displacing established systems such as Intapp conflicts software. He explicitly grounds the easier-entry argument in personal experience. He also warns that branding every module Clio risks a failing component damaging perceptions of the entire platform.
qs: when it comes to matter management software, big firms are sorely missing in that area.
that’s probably going to be their entry into large firms because that’s not going to be replacing anything.
It’s not Operate that doesn’t work, it’s Clio that doesn’t work.

kp.k: AI could initiate workflows rather than merely collect intake
kp.d: Lambert describes capabilities on the horizon for Clio and other vendors: once a matter is opened, AI could identify required documents, begin drafting them, map processes and calendar filing and follow-up dates. This is prospective assistant-style automation, not a demonstrated deployment or a claim that lawyers can rely on outputs without supervision.
qs: one of the things that I was hearing that is on the horizon for ⁓ a Clio and others is that once a matter is set up of using AI to then start the Workflow and the process mapping
instead of just saying you need those five documents of actually starting to draft those five documents and give you something to work with
here are the dates that you have to get this in by. Here’s your time to follow up.

kp.k: Workflow automation depends on integrations and practice-specific processes
kp.d: Asked how AI would know which documents to prepare, Lambert offers a tentative explanation involving document management systems, Outlook, courts, dockets and jurisdiction-specific secondary-source checklists. Gebauer considers the proposal plausible if those connections exist, but stresses that bespoke processes, even within practice groups, require more narrowly tailored automation.
qs: I don’t know that I can answer it.
tapped into the courts, tapped into the dockets.
it could work if it’s connected all of that.
subgroups of practice groups have, have, you know, their own types of processes.

kp.k: Legal research improvements attributed to better retrieval infrastructure
kp.d: Lambert reports substantial improvements in legal research outputs over the past five or six months after a couple of years of poor results. He recounts Ed Walters attributing improvement partly to stronger models but especially to RAG, vector databases and technologists’ improved understanding. Lambert’s subsequent research highlights indexing, chunking and retrieval of better source material. These are practitioner observations and a reported technical explanation, without comparative performance measurements in the transcript.
qs: with the legal research products over the past five or six months. And that is a substantial improvement in output.
He says, but really what’s going on is behind the scenes. And that is that the RAG technology and the vector databases have significantly improved.
the technologists have better understandings on how to work ⁓ with that.
a lot of it is on how the data in the vector databases is being indexed and it’s being chopped up or chunked

kp.k: Poor outputs previously undermined confidence in human checking
kp.d: Gebauer describes reluctance to use legal research AI when she could not trust herself to catch errors. Lambert argues vendors benefited from attorneys’ unusually extended tolerance because users expected improvement. Their exchange describes trust and verification burdens rather than measured error rates.
qs: you’re just like I’m just not gonna use this because I don’t trust that I’ll catch it.
a lot of attorneys had a very long runway of forgiveness
I think everyone thought this was going to improve

kp.k: In-house AI discussions emphasize risk more than operational enablement
kp.d: Gebauer’s account of ACC emphasizes governance, regulation and protection against improper generative AI use. She heard only one panel briefly address data governance, hygiene and cleanup as prerequisites for effective AI, and relatively little about helping organizations use tools safely and effectively. She qualifies her observations: this was her first ACC, she missed Monday because of travel disruption and attended only AI programs.
qs: lots of the presentations were about AI and generative AI.
you have to have a data governance policy.
data hygiene and data cleanup in order to make
I only went to the AI programs.

kp.k: Outside firms can supply clients with AI implementation expertise
kp.d: Gebauer recommends that in-house teams tap panel firms’ innovation, knowledge management and data science expertise. She reports audience demand for concrete examples and benchmarking, disputes a panel assertion that benchmarking does not exist, and points to available evaluations without supplying identifiable study details or results. She also sees conferences such as ACC as opportunities for firms to demonstrate how their technology work benefits clients.
qs: There’s an ability to reach out to your panel firms and your outside council because they have lots of people in this space, an innovation space or a knowledge management space or data science.
They have a lot of this knowledge. So tap into that if you can.
they were very hungry for examples
There’s plenty of opportunity for law firms to go and showcase what they’re doing in this technology space and how it’s benefiting the clients.

kp.k: Providing appropriate tools can reduce shadow AI incentives
kp.d: Gebauer reports strong concern at ACC that employees do not understand what information is safe to put into an LLM or why. She recommends that legal departments act as organizational partners in supplying needed tools, arguing that employees otherwise turn elsewhere. This frames governance as enabling appropriate use as well as restricting unsafe behavior.
qs: There’s this deep fear that people
don’t really understand, you know, when they’re, you know, putting stuff into an LLM, like what’s safe, what’s not, why it’s safe, why it’s not.
Lots of concerns about shadow AI
because if they don’t have them, right, they’ll go someplace else.

kp.k: AI governance policies require frequent revision across jurisdictions
kp.d: Gebauer argues that divergent and rapidly changing jurisdictional rules make in-house governance difficult. She characterizes AI policies as fluid documents that might remain useful for six months rather than a year before revision. Lambert emphasizes the additional difficulty of governing organizations with tens of thousands of employees across many jurisdictions; these are illustrative scale concerns, not a reported organizational sample.
qs: some of them kind of take different positions. Some of them are much more relaxed, others are not.
It’s changing, changing really rapidly.
That’s not gonna be something that you’re gonna rely on for a year. You’re gonna rely on it for maybe six months, and then you’re gonna have to change it again.

kp.k: Vendor imitation shapes the diffusion of legal technology
kp.d: Lambert argues that vendors, like law firms, often prefer following rather than pioneering. He cites Casetext innovations followed by similar offerings from Lexis, Westlaw, Bloomberg and others as his example. This is a practitioner characterization of competitive behavior rather than a systematic market study.
qs: No one wants to go first, but no one wants to go third.
when you see big ideas coming out from one vendor, you know the others are taking notes and ready to follow.
Case text would come out with something cool. Lexis and Westlaw and Bloomberg and others would come out with the same product.

kp.k: Clio explores customer experience through brain-wave monitoring
kp.d: Lambert recounts a Clio conference presentation combining customer work data with a process in which customers wore caps to monitor brain waves while working, examining frustration and enjoyment. The transcript provides no sample size, protocol, findings or evidence of AI’s measured effects; its substantive contribution is the reported approach to understanding legal software users’ experience.
qs: They literally had a process where they had customers that had the cap.
had the cap on their head to test their brain waves while they were working.
they did a number of things to see kind of how they were approaching things, what kind of frustrated them, they found joy.

kp.k: Susskind frames AI as assistance amid unmet legal demand
kp.d: Lambert characterizes Richard Susskind’s closing keynote as relatively optimistic about AI and continuing opportunities in legal services despite increasingly capable tools. He reports Susskind’s criticism of how services are sold, hope for moving beyond hourly billing and emphasis on unmet demand. This is Lambert’s account of Susskind’s position, not a direct quotation from Susskind, and supplies no quantified demand estimate or pricing transition timetable.
qs: his big thing is the way we sell services is not great.
there’s still hope that we’ll get off the billable hour sometime.
even as they get smarter, there’s still a lot of opportunity in the legal field.
there’s so much, know, demand, pent up demand for legal services that go unmet.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Publicly searchable ChatGPT conversations can expose lawyers, clients and sensitive strategies.
pts.d: Cheryl Wilson Griffin describes an exposure of shared ChatGPT conversations and alleges that one conversation enabled identification of a lawyer and a multinational energy client, while revealing a proposed strategy to exploit indigenous landowners' lack of knowledge of land value. She characterises this as 'searchable malpractice'; the transcript does not report a malpractice adjudication.

pts.k: Legal AI research output has improved substantially, with better retrieval and data preparation offered as important causes.
pts.d: Greg Lambert reports his own observation of improved legal research outputs. Separately, Ed Walters's explanation, relayed by Lambert rather than directly interviewed here, credits improvements in RAG, vector databases and technologists' understanding of them, alongside better models. Lambert elaborates that indexing, chunking and retrieval now better isolate relevant source material.

pts.k: AI may turn matter intake into proactive drafting, workflow initiation and deadline management.
pts.d: Lambert describes a prospective capability for Clio and other providers: after a matter is opened, AI would identify required documents, begin drafting them and populate filing and follow-up dates. This is framed as assistant-type support that gives lawyers something to work with, rather than autonomous legal service delivery.

pts.k: Clio's AI-associated expansion may enter Big Law through unmet matter-management needs rather than replacement of incumbent systems.
pts.d: Lambert describes Clio's move beyond its traditional small-firm base and predicts Clio Operate could provide the entry point into large firms. His argument is that filling an apparent product gap is easier than displacing an entrenched conflicts system. This is a software-vendor market claim, not an ALSP claim.

pts.k: AI creates an opportunity for outside firms to help corporate legal departments through technical expertise and practical examples.
pts.d: Gebauer argues that in-house teams can draw on panel firms' innovation, knowledge-management and data-science capabilities. She also sees a marketing opportunity for law firms to demonstrate client benefits. She reports audience interest in examples and benchmarking, but supplies no benchmark results.

pts.k: AI governance requires enabling approved use as well as managing risk, and policies will need frequent revision.
pts.d: Gebauer argues that employees will seek tools elsewhere if their organisation does not provide what they need, creating shadow-AI concerns. She predicts that rapidly changing, inconsistent jurisdictional requirements make governance policies fluid rather than annual set-and-forget documents.

pts.k: AI assistance can coexist with substantial opportunities for legal work because demand remains unmet.
pts.d: Richard Susskind's position, as paraphrased by Lambert from his keynote, is that smarter AI tools can assist lawyers while considerable opportunity remains. Lambert also reports Susskind's dissatisfaction with how legal services are sold and hope for moving beyond hourly billing. These are secondhand attributed positions, not direct Susskind quotations or predictions of imminent lawyer elimination.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Wilson Griffin offers a reported exposure count and a specific conversation example.
pts.d: She reports at least 110,000 exposed conversations and directs listeners to her team's Legal Tech Hub article. The transcript supplies neither the underlying count methodology nor independent documentation of the identification claim.

pts.k: The improvement claim rests on personal experience, a vendor expert's explanation and unspecified technical research.
pts.d: Lambert cites a hallway conversation with Walters of vLex and his own subsequent research. No named product comparison, quantitative accuracy result or reproducible benchmark is presented for the improvement claim.

pts.k: This is a conference-derived roadmap claim, not a demonstrated performance finding.
pts.d: Lambert reports what he heard was on the horizon and acknowledges uncertainty about how document selection would work. Gebauer draws on her own workflow work to assess its conditional feasibility.

pts.k: Lambert bases the market prediction on conference plans and his own implementation experience.
pts.d: He cites the vLex acquisition, reported funding of $900 million and his perception of a matter-management gap. No large-firm sales results or adoption data are offered.

pts.k: The partnership claim derives from Gebauer's limited ACC attendance and panel participation.
pts.d: She reports strong demand for examples and benchmarking and comparatively little discussion of partnering with outside counsel. Her recollection of specific benchmarking resources is uncertain, so it does not establish a named evaluation result.

pts.k: The governance claims reflect conference concerns and professional judgment.
pts.d: Gebauer reports worries about employees not understanding safe LLM use and the difficulty of managing differing regulations. No survey, measured shadow-AI prevalence or specific regulatory comparison is provided.

pts.k: The opportunity claim is a secondhand summary of a keynote, supported by an assertion of unmet demand.
pts.d: The transcript offers no demand figures, access-to-justice measurements or pricing evidence. Lambert describes the position as consistent with Susskind's longstanding arguments.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reported exposure became known the previous month and concerned conversations made public through a checkbox.
pts.d: The timing is relative to the episode, not a specified calendar date. Wilson Griffin says indexing and archival capture made the exposure enduring. Her account concerns publicly exposed conversations, not a claim that all private ChatGPT conversations were searchable.

pts.k: Lambert locates the improvement in the preceding five or six months, following years of poor results.
pts.d: The causal explanation makes better retrieval of suitable source data central; neither speaker claims that errors have disappeared or that human verification is unnecessary.

pts.k: The capability is prospective and depends on connected systems and practice-specific processes.
pts.d: No release date is given. Lambert suggests integration with document management, Outlook, courts, dockets and jurisdiction-specific checklists. Gebauer qualifies feasibility by noting that firms and practice subgroups have bespoke processes requiring narrower configuration.

pts.k: The large-firm entry is a qualified prediction without a deadline.
pts.d: Lambert says 'probably' and conditions the opportunity on supplying a new process or product rather than replacing existing infrastructure. He describes the acquisition as still awaiting what he believes is a Spanish approval.

pts.k: The partnership opportunity is immediate but depends on access to relevant firm expertise.
pts.d: Gebauer presents outreach as a present option rather than a forecast of universal collaboration. She also stresses data hygiene and cleanup as prerequisites for effective internal AI use.

pts.k: Gebauer suggests policies may need changing after roughly six months.
pts.d: The six-month interval is a tentative practical prediction tied to rapid change, not a formal compliance deadline. The shadow-AI prediction is conditional on employees lacking needed approved tools.

pts.k: The outlook is open-ended and remains optimistic as AI becomes smarter.
pts.d: No date is given for expanded service provision or departure from hourly billing. The framing is augmentation through assistance, not direct reliance on autonomous output.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Lawyers and clients face disclosure and reputational risks; counterparties may discover strategies directed against them.
pts.d: Wilson Griffin presents the risk as both personal and professional. Her legal example concerns an Austin lawyer, a multinational energy client and indigenous landowners.

pts.k: Lawyers using legal research tools may obtain more useful outputs, while vendors depend on better retrieval engineering.
pts.d: Marlene Gebauer describes prior reluctance to use tools when she could not trust herself to catch errors. The discussion links improved output to potential usability, without measuring changes in adoption or lawyer productivity.

pts.k: Matter teams could receive draft documents and organised next steps immediately after client engagement.
pts.d: The proposed change concerns intake and matter execution across lawyers and their supporting teams. The transcript supplies no quantified time savings or staffing-reduction prediction.

pts.k: Large law firms become a target beyond Clio's small and solo customers.
pts.d: The predicted shift affects Clio's customer market and large firms' operational tooling; Lambert distinguishes this opportunity from competing directly with incumbent conflicts vendors.

pts.k: Corporate legal buyers may gain implementation support, while outside firms can demonstrate differentiated value.
pts.d: The roles remain distinct: in-house counsel are organisational advisers and buyers; outside firms supply legal and technical expertise; innovation, knowledge-management and data-science teams are potential collaborators.

pts.k: In-house counsel and general counsel face ongoing organisation-wide governance burdens.
pts.d: Gebauer positions legal departments as partners helping employees use AI safely and effectively. Lambert highlights the scale challenge in multinational organisations with many employees and jurisdictions.

pts.k: Legal practitioners retain opportunities, and people with unmet legal needs are potential beneficiaries.
pts.d: The keynote summary connects assistance to unmet legal demand but does not identify particular underserved populations or demonstrate that AI has already reduced the justice gap. Its use of 'leverage' concerns assistance, not a reported change in associate-to-partner ratios.
